items.rationale: The difference is who owns the control flow: in a workflow the code fixes the order of steps, in an agent the model decides what happens next. Option a shows the belief that tool use is what makes something an agent (M11, that using tools or models in the steps makes a system an agent); b mixes up who runs a tool with who decides the next step (M14); d treats the number of model calls as the dividing line (M15).

The code fixes the three steps and their order, so it is a workflow, even though models are used inside two of the steps. Picking a or c shows M11, the belief that using a tool or a model inside the steps makes a system an agent; b shows M15, the belief that several model calls make an agent.

An agent loops until it decides to stop, so a request takes more model calls, and how many is not known in advance; a workflow has a fixed, small number. An answer about the agent using a bigger or smarter model misses that the extra cost comes from the loop.

In a workflow the path is fixed, so you can test each step alone and know which step failed. Option b shows M17, the belief that model calls give identical text every time; c shows M18, the belief that an agent cannot be tested at all because its output varies; d shows M19, the belief that a fixed workflow needs no real testing.

The steps are known and always in the same order, so code can own the flow and loop over the bookings, with the model only writing each message. Option a shows M20, the belief that varied wording means the model must own the control flow; b shows M20 too, that any step needing judgment means the model must own the control flow; d shows M21, the belief that a changing amount of data needs an agent, when a program loop handles it.

When the next step depends on what comes back and the paths cannot be listed in advance, the model has to own the control flow, so an agent fits; a limit on its work keeps the cost bounded. Option a tries to write out a fixed workflow for a task whose paths are too many to list (M22, the belief that a workflow can be made to fit any task); c runs every tool every time, wasting budget on requests that need fewer (also M22); d removes the limit that protects the budget.
